Hospital day 3 endocrinology progress note for a 71-year-old female with long-standing type 1 diabetes on an insulin pump, admitted after a severe hypoglycemic episode. She works rotating night shifts at a part-time warehouse job, so her meal timing and sleep vary widely from week to week. Three days ago a coworker found her sweaty, shaky and confused during a night shift, and the paramedics measured a fingerstick glucose of 38 mg/dL. She improved after intravenous dextrose and was admitted for monitoring and pump adjustment. She reports about four symptomatic lows each week over the past two months, mostly in the early morning after her shift, and she often does not feel them until she is quite low. Overnight in the hospital she had one asymptomatic low of 62 mg/dL on her continuous glucose monitor and treated it with juice. She denies chest pain, palpitations, seizure activity, or focal weakness, and she denies any head strike or fall.

Her history includes hypertension, hypothyroidism, hyperlipidemia, stage 3a chronic kidney disease, and diabetic peripheral neuropathy. Home medications are insulin lispro by continuous subcutaneous infusion, levothyroxine 75 mcg daily, lisinopril 10 mg daily, and atorvastatin 40 mg nightly. She also uses several over-the-counter supplements. She first told me she takes chromium picolinate 200 mcg twice daily, but after reading the bottle label she corrected this to 500 mcg once daily. She also takes cinnamon capsules every day, dose unknown, and alpha-lipoic acid 600 mg daily. She has no known drug allergies.

Vitals this morning are temperature 36.8 C, heart rate 74, blood pressure 138/76, respiratory rate 16, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. She is alert, oriented and comfortable. Mucous membranes are moist, heart sounds are regular without a murmur, lungs are clear, and the abdomen is soft and non-tender. The pump infusion site on the left abdomen is clean without redness. Monofilament sensation is reduced over both feet, unchanged from her baseline.

Data review: arrival glucose was 38 mg/dL and HbA1c is 6.4%. Creatinine is 1.3 with an eGFR of 44, potassium 4.4, and TSH 2.1. C-peptide is undetectable, in keeping with her known type 1 diabetes. CT of the head without contrast in the emergency department showed no acute findings. The continuous glucose monitor download shows 18% of readings below 70 mg/dL, concentrated between 4 and 9 in the morning, with the lowest values after correction boluses taken near the end of her shift.

Assessment is recurrent severe hypoglycemia with impaired awareness of hypoglycemia in a patient with type 1 diabetes on an insulin pump. This is likely multifactorial: overly aggressive basal and correction settings that do not fit her shifting schedule, reduced insulin clearance from her declining kidney function, and the glucose-lowering effect of her supplements. An HbA1c of 6.4% is lower than appropriate for her age and hypoglycemia history, so I am setting an individualized goal of 7.5 to 8%.

Today I will reduce the overnight basal rate from 0.85 to 0.65 units per hour and relax the correction factor. With her diabetes educator I will set up two pump profiles, one for work nights and one for days off. Stop chromium picolinate, cinnamon capsules and alpha-lipoic acid. Start glucagon 3 mg nasal powder as needed for severe hypoglycemia, and her daughter will be taught to use it. Continue levothyroxine, lisinopril and atorvastatin unchanged. Set the continuous glucose monitor low alert at 80 mg/dL. Dietitian visit before discharge, repeat basic metabolic panel in the morning, and endocrine clinic follow-up in two weeks. Anticipate discharge tomorrow if there are no further lows.

She also has hypertension, hypothyroidism, hyperlipidemia, stage 3a chronic kidney disease and diabetic peripheral neuropathy, and she uses several over-the-counter supplements. The assessment is recurrent severe hypoglycemia with impaired awareness, likely from aggressive pump settings, reduced insulin clearance and the supplements. The overnight basal rate was reduced, shift-specific pump profiles are being set up, the supplements are stopped, and nasal glucagon is started. Discharge is anticipated tomorrow if there are no further lows.

Telehealth video visit for urology follow-up. The patient joined by secure two-way video from her home, alone in a quiet room, and she is able to hear and see me without difficulty. This is a 70-year-old female with overactive bladder who also takes an anticoagulant. History is patient-reported and the examination is limited to what can be seen on video.

She has had urinary urgency and frequency for about a year, with urge incontinence two to three times a week and nocturia four times a night. She also reports dry mouth and constipation since starting oxybutynin several months ago. She first told me she takes oxybutynin 10 mg three times daily, then checked the bottle during the visit and corrected this to 5 mg twice daily. She denies dysuria, gross hematuria, fever, flank pain, or a feeling of incomplete emptying. She drinks about two liters of fluid a day and has tea in the evening.

Her past history includes atrial fibrillation, hypertension, and type 2 diabetes. Current medications are apixaban 5 mg twice daily, metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily, metformin 500 mg twice daily, furosemide 40 mg daily taken at 4 in the afternoon for ankle swelling that she says resolved months ago, and oxybutynin as above. She has no known drug allergies.

Home measurements this morning on her own cuff were blood pressure 128/76 and heart rate 66. On video she appears comfortable, speaks in full sentences, and has no respiratory distress. There is no visible swelling of the ankles when she raises her feet toward the camera. She is alert and follows instructions without difficulty.

Results reviewed: urinalysis from her primary care physician last week showed 5 to 10 red blood cells per high power field with negative nitrite and negative leukocyte esterase, and the urine culture showed no growth. Creatinine is 0.9 with an eGFR of 70, and HbA1c is 7.1%. A bladder scan at her last clinic visit showed a post-void residual of 40 mL.

Impression and plan. She has overactive bladder with urge incontinence and nocturia, with bothersome dry mouth and constipation on oxybutynin, which is also not an ideal drug at her age. She also has microscopic hematuria while on apixaban, which needs a full evaluation and should not be attributed to the anticoagulant alone. Stop oxybutynin. Start mirabegron 25 mg once daily. Mirabegron can raise blood pressure and can increase metoprolol levels, so she will check her blood pressure daily for two weeks and send the readings through the portal, and she will report a slow pulse or lightheadedness. Continue apixaban 5 mg twice daily without interruption. Order a renal and bladder ultrasound and refer her for cystoscopy to evaluate the microscopic hematuria. Reduce furosemide from 40 mg to 20 mg daily and take it in the morning, since the ankle swelling has resolved and the afternoon dose worsens nocturia; her primary care physician will be notified. Complete a three-day bladder diary and limit tea after dinner. Refer to pelvic floor physical therapy. Follow-up video visit in four weeks. She should call right away or go to the emergency department for gross blood in the urine, fever, flank pain, or inability to urinate.

The impression is overactive bladder with anticholinergic side effects and microscopic hematuria on apixaban. Oxybutynin was stopped, mirabegron 25 mg daily was started, furosemide was reduced to 20 mg daily, and apixaban continues. A renal and bladder ultrasound, cystoscopy referral, bladder diary and pelvic floor physical therapy were ordered, with video follow-up in four weeks.

Doctor: Welcome. I have a 60-year-old female here for a pre-operative cardiac evaluation before a right total knee replacement for severe knee osteoarthritis. Who is with you today?
Patient: This is my daughter. She keeps track of all my pills for me.
Family member: I fill her pill box and help with appointments, so I'll jump in if I need to.
Doctor: Perfect. Your chart lists high blood pressure, type 2 diabetes, and high cholesterol. Is that right?
Patient: Yes, that's right.
Doctor: Tell me what you've noticed with your heart and breathing lately.
Patient: Honestly, nothing much. I get a little winded on the stairs, but my knee is so bad I figured that was why.
Family member: She stops halfway up one flight to catch her breath. She didn't do that last year.
Doctor: How long has that been going on?
Patient: Maybe two or three months.
Doctor: Any chest pain or pressure with it?
Patient: No chest pain.
Doctor: Palpitations, fainting, or passing out?
Patient: No, nothing like that.
Doctor: Do you need extra pillows to sleep, or wake up gasping for air?
Patient: No, I sleep flat.
Doctor: Any leg swelling?
Patient: No, my ankles are fine.
Doctor: I see you just got back from overseas.
Patient: Yes, we flew home ten days ago from a family trip, about fourteen hours in the air with one stop.
Family member: Her left calf felt tight at the end of the flight, but it went away after a day or two.
Doctor: Is it still tight or swollen today?
Patient: No, it feels normal now.
Doctor: Any fever, cough, diarrhea, or vomiting since the trip?
Patient: No, I felt fine, just tired from the time change.
Doctor: Okay. Tell me about your medicines.
Patient: Let me think. There's the blood pressure pills. Amlodipine 10 mg, I think, and lisinopril.
Family member: Mom, I fill the box. The amlodipine is 5 mg, not 10. The lisinopril is 20 mg once a day.
Patient: Okay, 5 mg then. And metoprolol, 50 mg once a day.
Family member: Right, metoprolol succinate 50 mg. She takes metformin 1000 mg twice a day and empagliflozin 10 mg every morning for the sugar, and atorvastatin 20 mg at night.
Doctor: Thank you. Anything over the counter?
Patient: Ibuprofen for the knee, 400 mg twice a day.
Doctor: Any allergies to medicines?
Patient: No allergies.
Doctor: Do you smoke?
Patient: I quit fifteen years ago.
Doctor: Let me go over your exam. Blood pressure is 148/88, heart rate 72 and regular, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. I hear a soft 2 out of 6 systolic murmur at the upper right of the breastbone. Lungs are clear. No swelling in the neck veins, and your left calf is soft and not tender.
Patient: That's good to hear.
Doctor: Your ECG today shows a normal sinus rhythm with no ischemic changes. Your labs from last week show creatinine 0.9 with an eGFR of 72, potassium 4.2, hemoglobin 12.9, hemoglobin A1c 7.4%, and LDL 118.
Doctor: Here is my impression. A knee replacement is an intermediate-risk operation, and by the revised cardiac risk index you are low risk, because you don't have known heart disease, heart failure, stroke, or insulin-treated diabetes. But I'm concerned by the new shortness of breath on one flight of stairs and the murmur, so we shouldn't skip a closer look. The long flight also raises your clot risk, even though your calf is fine now.
Doctor: Here is the plan. First, I'm ordering an echocardiogram and an NT-proBNP blood test before surgery. Second, a venous ultrasound of the left leg to be safe. If both are normal, you can go ahead with surgery and I don't think you need a stress test. Third, stop the ibuprofen, because it can raise your blood pressure and strain your kidneys, and take acetaminophen 650 mg every six hours as needed instead. Fourth, increase atorvastatin from 20 mg to 40 mg at night because your LDL is high. Fifth, for surgery, continue metoprolol, skip lisinopril the morning of surgery, stop empagliflozin three days before, and hold metformin the day of surgery. Come back in two weeks to review the tests.
Patient: Okay, got it.
Family member: I'll write that down.
summary: A 60-year-old female with high blood pressure, type 2 diabetes and high cholesterol was seen for pre-operative cardiac evaluation before a right total knee replacement, accompanied by her daughter who helped with the history and medications. She has had new winded breathing on one flight of stairs for two to three months, a soft systolic murmur, and a long international flight ten days ago with transient left calf tightness. ECG showed normal sinus rhythm, and her revised cardiac risk is low. An echocardiogram, NT-proBNP and a left leg venous ultrasound were ordered, ibuprofen was stopped for acetaminophen, atorvastatin was increased to 40 mg, and perioperative medication instructions were given.

Neurology dictation, hospital day 3, on a 76-year-old female with relapsing remitting multiple sclerosis who was admitted with a suspected relapse. She was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis about twenty five years ago and has had two prior relapses, the last one eight years ago involving the left eye. About a week ago she developed numbness and weakness in the right leg with trouble walking, and over the next few days she noticed she was dragging the right foot and holding onto the walls at home. She also has bladder urgency and an electric shock sensation down her spine when she bends her neck forward. She denies fever, painful urination, headache, vision loss, double vision, difficulty swallowing, and new weakness in the arms. Because she has limited health literacy, I used plain language and teach-back with her throughout, and she describes her illness as her nerves getting angry again.

Her home medications are dimethyl fumarate 120 mg twice daily, correction, 240 mg twice daily, which I confirmed against the pharmacy list, baclofen 5 mg three times daily for leg stiffness, amlodipine 5 mg daily, and metformin 1000 mg twice daily. Past history also includes hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and osteoporosis. She has no known drug allergies.

On exam vitals are temperature 36.9 C, heart rate 78, blood pressure 152/84, respiratory rate 16, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. She is alert and oriented with fluent speech. Strength is 3 out of 5 at the right hip flexor and ankle dorsiflexion and 5 out of 5 elsewhere. Reflexes are brisk in the legs with an upgoing toe on the right. There is reduced vibration and pinprick sensation in the right leg below the knee, and she walks only with a walker and a right foot drop.

Data review. Urinalysis was negative for nitrite and leukocyte esterase and the urine culture shows no growth, so there is no infection to explain a pseudo-relapse. WBC is 8.2, creatinine 0.8, and her glucose was 246 mg/dL this morning on steroids. Her absolute lymphocyte count is 0.7, which is low. MRI of the brain and cervical spine with and without gadolinium showed a new enhancing lesion at C3-C4 on the right side of the cord and several old periventricular lesions without enhancement.

Impression is an acute relapse of multiple sclerosis with a right sided cervical cord lesion, a breakthrough on dimethyl fumarate, with lymphopenia and steroid associated hyperglycemia.

Recommendations and plan. Continue methylprednisolone 1000 mg IV daily for a total of five days, and today is dose three. Start pantoprazole 40 mg daily while she is on high dose steroids. Hold metformin while inpatient and start insulin lispro on a sliding scale with meals for the steroid associated hyperglycemia, with glucose checks before meals and at bedtime. Stop dimethyl fumarate because of the lymphopenia and the breakthrough relapse, and she will see the neuroimmunology clinic to discuss another disease modifying therapy. Increase baclofen from 5 mg to 10 mg three times daily for the leg stiffness. Order a bladder scan for post void residual, physical therapy and occupational therapy, and fall precautions. Pharmacy will make a picture based medication calendar and we will repeat teach-back with her before discharge. Anticipate discharge to home with outpatient therapy after the fifth dose of steroids, with MS clinic follow-up in two weeks.
summary: A 76-year-old female with relapsing remitting multiple sclerosis was admitted with a relapse causing right leg numbness and weakness, trouble walking, bladder urgency and an electric shock sensation down the spine; she has limited health literacy and teach-back was used. Urinalysis and culture were negative, and MRI showed a new enhancing C3-C4 cord lesion. The impression is an acute relapse with a cervical cord lesion and breakthrough on dimethyl fumarate, with lymphopenia and steroid associated hyperglycemia. Methylprednisolone continues for five days with pantoprazole, insulin lispro sliding scale, metformin held, baclofen increased to 10 mg three times daily, and dimethyl fumarate stopped. Therapy, a bladder scan, and neuroimmunology and MS clinic follow-up are planned.

Doctor: Good evening. What brings you in tonight?
Patient: I've had this cough for about three months now. It just won't go away.
Doctor: I see you are a 65-year-old male, and the nurse mentioned you work night shifts.
Patient: Yes, I'm a security guard on the overnight shift, so I come in whenever I can get away.
Doctor: Is the cough dry, or are you bringing up phlegm?
Patient: Dry, mostly. It tickles in my throat, and it's worse when I lie down to sleep in the morning.
Doctor: Any fever, shortness of breath, or coughing up blood?
Patient: No, none of those. And I haven't lost weight.
Doctor: Do you smoke?
Patient: Never.
Doctor: Any medical problems, and what do you take?
Patient: Just high blood pressure. I take lisinopril 20 mg once a day. I started it about four months ago.
Doctor: Okay. Your temperature is normal, your oxygen level is 98% on room air, your lungs sound clear, and your throat looks fine with no drainage. I think this cough is from the lisinopril, what we call an ACE inhibitor cough. It started not long after you began it.
Patient: Really? I didn't connect those.
Doctor: It's common. Here is the plan. Stop the lisinopril and start losartan 50 mg once a day for your blood pressure. We will get a chest X-ray today to make sure the lungs are healthy. The cough should settle over the next few weeks. Follow up with your regular doctor in two weeks, and come back sooner if you get a fever, shortness of breath, or cough up blood.
Patient: Okay, thank you.
summary: A 65-year-old male night-shift worker with high blood pressure presented with a dry cough for about three months that started shortly after he began lisinopril. He denies fever, shortness of breath, coughing up blood and weight loss, and he has never smoked. His lungs are clear and oxygen level is 98% on room air. The impression is an ACE inhibitor cough. Lisinopril was stopped and losartan 50 mg once a day was started, a chest X-ray was ordered, and he will follow up with his regular doctor in two weeks.

Cardiology consult dictation, hospital day 1, requested by orthopedics for pre-operative cardiac risk assessment in an 85-year-old female admitted after a mechanical fall at home with a right femoral neck fracture. Surgery is planned for tomorrow morning. She tripped on a rug and denies any dizziness or loss of consciousness before the fall. She has severe right hip pain. She denies chest pain, palpitations, shortness of breath at rest, orthopnea, and leg swelling. Before the fracture she walked with a cane and could climb one flight of stairs slowly without stopping, which is about four METs. Past history includes hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and a heart murmur known for several years. Home medications are lisinopril 10 mg daily, metoprolol succinate 25 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg daily, and aspirin 81 mg daily, and she has no known drug allergies. In the emergency department she was started on acetaminophen 650 mg every six hours for pain.

On exam blood pressure is 138/74, heart rate 70 and regular, respiratory rate 16, oxygen saturation 96% on room air, correction, 97% on room air. Jugular venous pressure is not elevated. There is a grade 2 out of 6 systolic ejection murmur at the right upper sternal border without radiation to the neck. Lungs are clear and there is no peripheral edema.

Data review. The ECG shows normal sinus rhythm with left ventricular hypertrophy by voltage and no acute ST changes. Troponin is negative. Creatinine is 1.0, potassium 4.1, and hemoglobin 11.8. An echocardiogram from last year showed an ejection fraction of 60% with mild aortic stenosis and a mean gradient of 18 mmHg.

Impression is a low to intermediate risk for a cardiac complication with hip fracture repair. Her revised cardiac risk index is zero, her functional capacity before the fall was about four METs, and she has no active cardiac condition such as unstable angina, decompensated heart failure, a significant arrhythmia, or severe valve disease. Her aortic stenosis is mild. Further cardiac testing would not change management and a delay in hip fracture surgery would increase her risk.

Recommendations to the primary team are to proceed with surgery as planned without further cardiac testing. Continue metoprolol succinate including the morning of surgery. Hold lisinopril the morning of surgery and resume it after surgery once her blood pressure and kidney function are stable. Continue atorvastatin and aspirin 81 mg daily. Keep her on telemetry perioperatively, avoid hypotension and large fluid shifts, and check a repeat ECG and troponin on postoperative days one and two. Cardiology will follow her after surgery.

The impression is a low to intermediate cardiac risk with no active cardiac condition. Surgery should proceed without further testing, continuing metoprolol, atorvastatin and aspirin, holding lisinopril on the morning of surgery, and monitoring with telemetry and a repeat ECG and troponin after surgery.

Dermatology follow-up for an 85-year-old female with hidradenitis suppurativa who has had recurrent painful lumps in both armpits and the groin for many years. She also has well controlled hypertension that is managed by her primary care physician. She reports three painful nodules in the right armpit and two in the groin that drain intermittently, with pain up to 6 out of 10 at worst. She has been using clindamycin 1% lotion twice daily for the last three months with only partial benefit. She denies fever, chills, and new lesions under the breasts or on the buttocks.

On exam there are several inflammatory nodules and two draining sinus tracts in the right axilla, and scarring with two tender nodules in both inguinal folds. There is no fluctuant abscess that needs drainage and no surrounding cellulitis.

Assessment is moderate hidradenitis suppurativa, Hurley stage II, with a partial response to topical therapy. Plan is to start doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 12 weeks, taken with food and a full glass of water while sitting upright, and to continue clindamycin 1% lotion twice daily. I advised sun protection while on doxycycline, loose-fitting clothing, gentle washing with a chlorhexidine wash, and warm compresses for painful nodules. Return in 12 weeks to assess response, and sooner if she develops fever, spreading redness, or a large painful abscess.
